item.title: Cross-party interest in Australian nuclear future, poll suggests
item.description: A YouGov poll commissioned by grassroots organisation Nuclear for Australia suggests that almost two-thirds of Australians believe nuclear should be considered as part of the nation's energy future.
item.wnn:fullText:
Of the 1550 people polled between 6-12 October, 63% believe Australia should consider nuclear power. Nearly as many - 60% - believe nuclear power will be part of Australia's future energy mix, while 59% support developing nuclear power in Australia to strengthen the nation's energy sovereignty. Just over half - 56% - support removing Australia's legislative restrictions to allow nuclear energy to be considered.

The poll also revealed concerns about Australia's ability to meet its electricity needs, with 57% of those polled saying they are not confident Australia's existing electricity options can meet growing demand from artificial intelligence, data centres and electrification. 

Support for nuclear was found across political lines, Australia for Nuclear said, with 48% of Labor voters and 44% of Green voters believing nuclear should be considered. 54% of Labor voters, and 70% of Coalition voters, expect it to form part of the nation's future energy mix. (The Australian Labor Party is Australia's current governing party, while the Liberal-National Coalition, a long-running alliance of the Liberal Party of Australia and the National Party - the main opposition). 

Nuclear for Australia was founded in 2022 by pro-nuclear activist Will Shackel, who was 16 at the time. The board of the organisation - which is a registered charity in Australia - is chaired by Adrian Paterson, former CEO of the Australian nuclear science and technology organisation ANSTO.

Australia has mined uranium since the mid-1950s but - despite ANSTO's long experience operating research reactors, and a significant infrastructure to support it - uses no nuclear power. With huge coal resources and significant amounts of natural gas, its electricity generation has been reliant on fossil fuels. There are several legal hurdles that would impede any consideration of nuclear power, including the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999 and Australian Radiation Protection and Nuclear Safety Act 1988, federal legislation that would need to be amended to remove prohibitions against effective regulation of nuclear power.


Will Shackel (Image: Nuclear for Australia)

Shackel said the poll "overwhelmingly" shows that Australians want all energy options on the table, including nuclear, and its findings should be a "wake-up call" for policymakers.

"In an increasingly uncertain world, energy sovereignty matters more than ever. Australia needs an affordable, reliable and clean energy grid to support its economy and attract investment in AI and data centres. Nuclear energy is not about choosing between nuclear and renewables. It's about making sure Australia has the energy mix it needs for the future. Nuclear is the only carbon-free baseload option to support renewables," he said.

"Lifting the legislative bans wouldn't mean committing Australia to new nuclear power plants tomorrow, but simply allow nuclear energy to be properly considered, assessed and debated alongside other technologies."

Paul Smith of YouGov said the research provided a detailed picture of Australians' attitudes towards nuclear energy.

"What stands out in these findings is the breadth of views across different voting groups. The results show that attitudes towards nuclear energy cannot simply be reduced to traditional political divisions."

YouGov is a member of the Australian Polling Council and has published a methodology statement for the poll.

item.title: Floating nuclear power plant 'has boosted air quality'
item.description: An environmental monitoring report for Russia's floating nuclear power plant suggests that emissions have fallen almost 80% since it started supplying heating in the area in 2022.
item.wnn:fullText:
According to the operators of the Akademik Lomonosov floating nuclear power plant in Chukotka, on eastern Russia's Arctic coast (pictured above), "after transferring a significant portion of the city's heating load to the floating nuclear power plant, gross emissions of pollutants into the atmosphere decreased almost fivefold - from 11.64 to 2.281 tonnes".

There are 11 automated radiation monitoring stations, plus four in the city of Pevek - population of 5,000 - as part of the environmental monitoring.

The report says that measurements of air emissions, water discharges, soil impacts and waste generation "all comply with established standards. On average, these levels are less than 10% of the maximum permissible values".

According to Russia's state nuclear corporation Rosatom, monitoring of the Chaunskaya Bay in the East Siberian Sea also shows no significant changes. This means, they say, the ecosystem is not experiencing any negative impact from the nuclear power plant.

Chukotka Governor Vladislav Kuznetsov said: "The environmental agenda is our region's number one priority. The Arctic is a fragile and vulnerable territory, and we must work here with particular attention to nature, human health, and the future of Pevek."

Dzhumberi Tkebuchava, First Deputy Director General of Rosenergoatom, said: "The floating nuclear power plant is of great importance for Chukotka and the Russian Arctic. It is a unique energy facility, closely monitored by the entire international community … the industrial environmental monitoring system at each of our nuclear power plants is evolving and improving year after year, as evidenced by the annual improvement in their environmental impact."

The Akademik Lomonosov

The Akademik Lomonosov began commercial operation in May 2020 and is the world's only operating floating nuclear power plant. It is based, with its coastal infrastructure, by the city of Pevek to which it supplies heat and power.

The Akademik Lomonosov has two KLT-40S reactors generating 35 MWe each, which are similar to those used in a previous generation of nuclear-powered icebreakers. It is also providing energy for the development of mining of the Baimskaya ore zone. It has the capacity to provide electricity to a city with a population of up to 100,000 people.

Rosatom is in the process of constructing four floating power units and is targeting the export market for floating nuclear power plants with capacity of at least 100 MWe and an assigned service life of up to 60 years featuring RITM-200M reactors, derived from those used on Russia's latest nuclear-powered icebreakers.
